title: Fireworks
objective: After this level you can explain how fireworks get their colors.
summary: Early fireworks were orange; colors came in the 1800s. Each comes from a metal whose heated electrons release light of its own color: strontium red, barium green, copper blue.

cards.headline: For centuries, fireworks came in one color.
cards.body: Fireworks go back more than 1,000 years, most likely to China. For centuries after that, they glowed only orange and gold, like sparks from a campfire. Then chemistry got hold of the palette.

cards.headline: Red, green, blue: pick a metal
cards.body: In the 1800s, chemists began adding newly made compounds and got reds, greens, blues and purples. Each color comes from a particular metal: strontium glows red, barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow. Mix two and you get blends, like copper and strontium for lavender. A firework's palette is really a list of elements.

cards.headline: Why each metal has its own color
cards.body: The heat of the burning firework gives electrons in the metal atoms extra energy, bumping them up to higher energy levels. They don't stay there. As they drop back down, they give that energy off as light. The size of the drop sets the color, and each element has its own drops. That's why strontium reliably means red: it's a fingerprint written in light.

mascot.line: Keep this: the color comes from electrons dropping back down, and each element drops its own way.

cards.headline: Blue, the hard one
cards.body: Blue is the most difficult firework color to produce. For a long time a "blue" firework was really an anemic bluish white. Only over recent decades have fireworks makers managed a true azure. So next time you watch a show, look for a deep, honest blue. It's the hardest trick in the sky.

cards.headline: Firework colors: explained
learned: Early fireworks glowed only orange and gold
Strontium red, barium green, copper blue, sodium yellow
Heated electrons fall back and release colored light
Blue is the hardest color to make

questions.prompt: Fireworks get their red color from _____.
questions.explanation: Strontium produces red; barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow.

questions.prompt: Match each firework metal with the color it glows.
questions.explanation: Strontium glows red, barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow.

questions.prompt: Using Level 57, where does the energy that lights up firework colors come from?

options.label: Cold absorbed by an endothermic process
options.rationale: Endothermic changes take heat in, not give it out.

options.label: Heat released by burning, an exothermic reaction
Sunlight stored in the metal during the day
options.rationale: Fireworks shine at night from their own reaction.

options.label: Electricity from a battery inside
options.rationale: The energy comes from a chemical reaction.

questions.explanation: Burning is exothermic; its heat excites the metal atoms' electrons, which then give off colored light.
